stories.headline: Nvidia Lost Hundreds of Billions in Market Value After Its CEO Admitted an Affair With an Alleged Chinese Spy. Shareholders Sued Within Minutes.
stories.lede: Nvidia's stock fell 4.3% Monday after CEO Jensen Huang confessed to an affair.
stories.truths: Huang's Memo Confirmed the Affair. The Lawsuit Arrived Before the Market Closed Its Books. Nvidia's stock closed down 4.3% on Monday and kept sinking Tuesday morning, a day after Jensen Huang told employees in a memo that he had been unfaithful to his wife ( Los Angeles Times ). By Tuesday the shares were down 10% from the pre-scandal close, and Huang, 63, had apologized to his wife and children in the same memo. A shareholder then filed a lawsuit seeking class action status, alleging that Nvidia "made false and misleading statements" about the CEO's interactions with Alice Huang ( ABC News ). The Daily Mail's headline put the delay between the closing bell and the complaint at five minutes. Nvidia's board answered with an independent committee, outside counsel and a statement of confidence in Huang. It also said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." That sentence has a problem, and the board's own position explains it. Huang says he has more than 60 direct reports, and analysts agree no successor has been named. Harvard Business School's David Yoffie called the board's position "between a rock and a hard spot" ( Houston Chronicle ). The committee is investigating the one person it cannot afford to remove. The Relationship Reached Back Further Than the Memo, and It Ran Through the Customer List. The affair is the part Huang has admitted. The business timeline is the part investigators care about. A photo confirmed by The New York Times shows Alice Huang with Jensen Huang at an Italian restaurant in Singapore in December 2023. She had just restructured Megaspeed, the company that would soon buy billions of dollars of Nvidia chips. Washington had barred Chinese buyers from those chips, and she had routed around the ban through a Singaporean shell company ( The New York Times ). Four days after the ownership change, Megaspeed was named an Nvidia cloud partner, which gave it access to the coveted components. Her résumé adds a detail the Financial Times found. She spent nearly a decade working alongside Kang Wei, a financier who was her romantic partner and who drew repeated fines from Chinese securities regulators ( Financial Times ). Nvidia's partner vetting, in other words, had a lot of public record to read. That Is Why a Personal Scandal Became a Policy Fight in One Weekend. The affair would have been a bad week. The Megaspeed timeline made it a bigger problem because Huang spent years as the most effective voice against tighter chip export rules, with, as Semafor put it, Trump's ear. His argument was that keeping China hooked on American hardware preserved the American lead. The hawks always called that self-serving. The facts now give them something to cite ( Semafor ). The first moves came within hours. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, and Sen. Jim Banks, a Republican, called on Congress to pass their AI Overwatch Act, and Rep. Bill Foster pressed for his Chip Security Act ( Al Jazeera ). Sen. Chris Coons, the incoming Foreign Relations chair, pointed the scandal at the White House. Meanwhile Trump, who has been briefed by someone, told reporters he did not say when. He called Huang a "fine person" and added, "you never know what is going on." Investors have started pricing a company without its founder. The Financial Times put that figure at roughly 30% of Nvidia's pre-scandal value, and the market has so far taken back a third of it.

page.title: The Megaspeed Chip Trail
page.contest: Whether Nvidia's board can credibly investigate a founder it cannot replace, and whether his ties to a buyer of restricted chips justify tighter export rules.
page.stakes: Investors have begun pricing a company without its founder, a loss the Financial Times put near 30% of pre-scandal value, while a shareholder class action tests what Nvidia told them. Lawmakers and the White House must decide whether export limits, long resisted by Huang, now need tightening.
page.here: Nvidia fell 4.3% Monday after Huang's memo and was down 10% by Tuesday, and a board committee now investigates the chief executive it cannot easily replace.

stories.headline: The US Pulled 10 Refueling Tankers Off RAF Mildenhall in a Single Day. Officials Still Can't Say What They Were Running From.
stories.lede: US forces moved tankers off a second UK base Monday over an unspecified Iran threat.
stories.truths: Ten Tankers Left Mildenhall in One Day, and the Pentagon Won't Say Why Flight-tracking data shows 10 US Air Force KC-135 tankers left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk on Monday. Two flew to Germany and Italy first. One circled Spangdahlem airbase in Germany, headed back toward Mildenhall without landing, held over Suffolk for nearly an hour, then flew east and landed at Spangdahlem after all. Later departures went to Spangdahlem, Ramstein and four to Morón in southern Spain, and three Ospreys left as well ( BBC ). A tanker that circles back, holds, and then lands somewhere else looks like a plan being revised mid-flight. The stated reason came secondhand. The Wall Street Journal reported the departures followed an Iranian threat, and the BBC could not verify that independently. The nature of the threat "remains under discussion among US officials," and the base protection level at Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath went to FPCON Charlie, the second-highest tier, which applies when intelligence says terrorist action is likely ( Al Jazeera ). On the record, the Air Force offered only that aircraft "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons," and declined to say more for operations security ( ABC News ). A routine rotation does not usually come with a force protection upgrade. Britain's answer was shorter still. The prime minister's spokesperson said the US is "one of our top security partners," and when asked whether British bases are safe, replied "Yes" ( The Guardian ). The Ministry of Defence said it does not routinely comment on other nations' activity. Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary challenged the reassurance publicly, according to the BBC. Downing Street is vouching for the safety of a base the ally that uses it just emptied. The First Base Already Taught Both Governments How This Goes None of this started Monday. In September, seven men were detained near RAF Fairford; two were later charged under the National Security Act, and prosecutors alleged one likely tried to assist Iranian intelligence inside the UK ( ABC News ). Washington pulled its B-1 bombers out of Fairford in October. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month the Fairford activity was likely coordinated in Iran, and Tehran's ambassador denied any plot. The Revolutionary Guard had said in July that Fairford and any base used to launch attacks on Iran were legitimate targets ( Al Jazeera ). The Pentagon's caution has a history behind it. Five KC-135 tankers, the same type that just left Mildenhall, were hit on the ground by an Iranian missile in Saudi Arabia in March. Officials have been risk averse about parked aircraft since. UK security officials, meanwhile, believe Iran lacks the capability for an explosive attack on a British base, though Tehran may threaten one to disrupt American calculations ( The Guardian ). So Washington is treating the bases as exposed while London says they are not, and neither side has shown the evidence. The decision on what comes next sits in the White House. Trump is weighing whether to resume bombing Iran, though he said overnight that further attacks were "highly unlikely" after last week's midterms, where Republicans were heavily defeated. Vice President JD Vance and other allies blamed the war for the losses ( The Guardian ). Tankers are what let bombers reach Iran from Britain. They are now parked in Germany, Spain and Scotland.

page.title: Iran War Reaches UK Bases
page.contest: Whether American aircraft based in Britain are exposed to Iranian retaliation, and whether London and Washington can agree on the danger without showing the evidence.
page.stakes: The US must decide where to park the tankers that let bombers reach Iran, while Britain must reassure its public that hosting them is safe. American crews, British communities near the bases, and any resumption of bombing all depend on that judgment.
page.here: On Monday ten US tankers left RAF Mildenhall over an unspecified Iranian threat, the second British base emptied, while both governments withheld evidence and Trump weighed resuming the bombing.

beginnings.line: Iran approved its constitution by referendum in December 1979, placing a supreme leader above the elected president and recognising the Revolutionary Guards.
Carter reported to Congress in April 1980 on a rescue mission that ended in the Iranian desert with eight American servicemen dead.
Trump signed a memorandum in May 2018 withdrawing the United States from the nuclear agreement and beginning a campaign of maximum pressure on Iran's economy.
Trump addressed the nation in June 2025 after the United States joined an Israeli air campaign, saying the strikes had destroyed key enrichment facilities.
Trump announced major combat operations in Iran at the end of February 2026, saying the aim was to eliminate imminent threats.

case.title: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (as amended 1989)
case.author: Islamic Republic of Iran
case.about: Approved by referendum in December 1979 and amended in 1989, the constitution placed a supreme leader above the elected president and parliament. It recognised the Revolutionary Guards as guardians of the revolution. Its structure explains why Iran's foreign policy answers to the supreme leader.

case.title: Report to Congress on the Faild Hostage Rescue Mission to Iran
case.author: Jimmy Carter
case.about: Carter sent the report in April 1980, after a rescue mission ended in the Iranian desert with eight American servicemen dead. The hostage crisis, begun when students seized the U.S. embassy in November 1979, set the hostility between the two governments that has lasted since.

case.title: National Security Presidential Memorandum on Ceasing United States Participation in the JCPOA
case.author: Donald J. Trump
case.about: The memorandum, signed in May 2018, withdrew the United States from the agreement and began a campaign of maximum pressure on Iran's economy. Iran later exceeded the deal's limits on enrichment. The collapse of the agreement is the background to the strikes that followed.

case.title: Address to the Nation on United States Airstrikes on Iran
case.author: Donald J. Trump
case.about: Trump addressed the nation from the White House in June 2025, after the United States joined an Israeli air campaign against Iran. He said the strikes had destroyed Iran's key enrichment facilities and warned Iran against retaliation. A ceasefire followed days later, but the question of Iran's program was not settled.

case.author: Donald J. Trump
case.about: Trump made the announcement at the end of February 2026, saying the objective was to eliminate imminent threats from the Iranian government. The joint American and Israeli campaign became a war that closed the Strait of Hormuz and drove up fuel prices worldwide. The page counts from this day.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine Sat Down in Abu Dhabi for Four Hours. The Real Item on the Table Was Europe's Borders, and Europe Wasn't Invited.
stories.lede: US envoys convened Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi for talks on a European security deal.
stories.truths: Four Hours in Abu Dhabi, and Neither President in the Room Russian and Ukrainian delegations met Tuesday for the first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months, and the session ran about four hours with a second day set for Wednesday ( PBS ). Neither Marco Rubio nor Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff ran the table, and Kushner told delegates the U.S. had "narrowed the gaps" without saying which ones ( AFP ). Rubio, speaking from a G7 meeting in Paris, called the day "very productive," then added that nothing was "on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours." Zelenskyy's account was narrower. His team spent much of the day on prisoner exchanges, captive civilians and children taken from Ukraine, along with security guarantees ( PBS ). Those are the topics where deals tend to happen first, and also the topics that cost the Kremlin least. The Agenda Moved Toward What Moscow Wanted Before the Invasion The bigger story sat behind the prisoner swaps. U.S. officials said Washington now believes a Ukraine deal requires a simultaneous agreement with Russia on Europe's future security, including a revived body modeled on the NATO-Russia Council ( Washington Post ). Observers called that a risky nod to a Russian goal. Months before the 2022 invasion, Moscow demanded that NATO pull its infrastructure out of Eastern Europe, and Sergei Ryabkov, the diplomat who delivered that ultimatum, sat in the Russian delegation Tuesday ( AFP ). Sergei Lavrov noticed what the Americans were offering. He praised the approach and contrasted it with the Biden administration, which he said refused to discuss collective security at all. Rubio supplied the condition that makes the praise understandable: any postwar guarantee for Ukraine has to be something Russia also accepts. That puts the Kremlin in an unusual spot. It may get a veto over the arrangement meant to deter it. Europe Got a Side Meeting The Europeans were handled in sequence. Officials from Germany, France, Britain, Italy, NATO and the EU met the Americans and Ukrainians before the Russians arrived, and then stood down ( Fox News ). Moscow has refused to see them at the main table. German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul said Europe "belongs at this table," and Rubio's answer was that it was not yet time ( ABC News ). The split also runs through Europe. Ursula von der Leyen wants broader security talks only after a ceasefire, while Lavrov wants the framework first and the war second, and he rejected a truce as a way to buy Ukraine breathing room ( ABC Australia ). Meanwhile, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit Ukraine overnight, 162 drones in all by Ukraine's count, and the power cuts came as temperatures fell ( PBS ). 162 drones and 1 ballistic missile Russia's overnight launch at Ukraine, hours before the delegations sat down. Rubio asked for patience. Ukraine's grid is getting the other kind of attention.

page.title: Europe's Security Order, Renegotiated
page.contest: Whether a settlement of the war in Ukraine can be separated from a wider bargain over European security that Russia has sought since before the invasion.
page.stakes: Ukraine's borders, its guarantees and the future of NATO's reach are at stake, as are the interests of European states excluded from the table. Moscow could gain a voice over the arrangements meant to deter it.
page.here: In Abu Dhabi, Russian and Ukrainian delegations met for four hours under US mediation, with a NATO-Russia style body on the agenda and European governments kept out.

beginnings.line: Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the Budapest Memorandum in 1994, pledging to respect Ukraine's borders as it joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
At the 2007 Munich security conference, Putin attacked a unipolar world led by the United States and objected to NATO enlargement and European missile defence.
In a televised address on the morning of the February 2022 invasion, Putin announced a special military operation, citing the demilitarisation and denazification of Ukraine.

case.title: Memorandum on Security Assurances in connection with Ukraine's accession to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (Budapest Memorandum)
case.author: Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States and Ukraine
case.about: Signed in Budapest in December 1994 by Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the memorandum accompanied Ukraine's accession to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The three states committed to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the threat or use of force against it. It gave assurances, not a defence guarantee.

case.title: Speech and the Following Discussion at the Munich Conference on Security Policy
case.author: Vladimir Putin
case.about: In February 2007 Putin used the annual Munich conference to attack what he called a unipolar world led by the United States. He objected to NATO's enlargement and to American plans for missile defence in Europe. Western officials later read the speech as an early warning of the course Russia would take.

case.title: Address by the President of the Russian Federation
case.author: Vladimir Putin
case.about: Putin announced what he called a special military operation in a televised address early on the morning of the invasion in February 2022. He said its aims were the demilitarisation and denazification of Ukraine. The address is the declaration that began the war this page counts from.

starts.line: In a televised address on the morning of the February 2022 invasion, Putin announced a special military operation, citing the demilitarisation and denazification of Ukraine.

page.why: The library's primary documents trace the Budapest assurances, the NATO-Russia council model, Moscow's objections to NATO growth, and the 2014 and 2022 acts that led to today's talks; the unrelated items were left out.

stories.headline: California's Billionaires Spent More Than $330 Million to Kill a $100 Billion Tax. Voters Who Sent Democrats to Congress Sided With Them.
stories.lede: California voters rejected Prop 40, a 5% billionaire tax, as Democrats won elsewhere.
stories.truths: Billionaires Outspent the Tax's Backers and Won the Biggest Ballot Fight on the Ticket Prop 40 would have charged roughly 200 California billionaires a one-time 5% tax on their wealth. Backers said it would raise about $100 billion over five years, most of it for healthcare after federal cuts in the Big Beautiful Bill. With about 60% of votes counted, "no" led 55.6% to 44.4% ( Al Jazeera ). The Associated Press called it Monday night. The money tells part of the story. Building a Better California, the main opposition group, raised $333.1 million this year. Sergey Brin of Google alone gave $102 million, and he gave it from Reno, Nevada, which is its own kind of argument about whether billionaires leave ( ABC News ). Berkeley economist Gabriel Zucman, one of the leading champions of wealth taxes, called the ad blitz "carpet-bombing" and said it could easily prove pivotal in a close contest ( NPR ). That explanation has a hole in it. Elon Musk put more than $150 million into defeating Democrat James Talarico in Texas, and Talarico won his Senate race comfortably ( NPR ). If money alone decides elections, Talarico loses. Something else was different in California. The Party That Proposed the Tax Split Over It The difference showed up inside the Democratic coalition. Gov. Gavin Newsom, a likely 2028 presidential candidate, came out against the measure, arguing billionaires could simply leave the state. He offered a counterproposal instead: a national tax aimed at loans billionaires take out against their assets ( ABC News ). Division among party leaders and labor unions drained early support before the vote ( Al Jazeera ). He doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors? Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., on Newsom Khanna, who campaigned for the measure alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, says he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both men have said they are weighing 2028 runs ( ABC News ). Prop 40 gave them a test run of the argument they will have in a primary, and the first round went to the side with the governor and the money. Washington Is Picking the Fight Up Anyway The loss stings the party's left wing, which had gained momentum from the midterm sweep that handed Democrats both chambers of Congress ( Al Jazeera ). It has not changed the plan in the Senate. Ron Wyden, the incoming Finance Committee chairman, said in a Nov. 4 statement that his panel would "redouble its efforts to ensure billionaires pay their fair share and hold tax cheats accountable" ( Al Jazeera ). Wyden's wording is the tell. He promised to chase tax cheats and to make billionaires pay their share. He did not promise a wealth tax. Whether the party's next fight is over a tax on wealth or a tax on borrowing against it may be the question California just handed to 2028.

page.title: Taxing the Very Rich
page.contest: Whether a state can tax the fortunes of its billionaires when their campaign money and the governor of the proposing party oppose the measure.
page.stakes: Roughly 200 California billionaires faced a one-time 5% levy meant to raise about $100 billion, mostly for healthcare after federal cuts. The outcome shapes who pays for that care and whether Democrats pursue taxes on wealth or on borrowing against it in 2028.
page.here: California voters rejected Prop 40, the 5% billionaire tax, while Democrats won elsewhere. The opposition raised $333.1 million, and Gov. Newsom sided against the measure.

stories.headline: Jimmy Carter's Family Farm Sold for $8.5 Million. It Becomes a 7,000-Acre Public Hunting Ground.
stories.lede: The Conservation Fund bought Carter's 2,500-acre Georgia farm to open it to the public.
stories.truths: The Conservation Fund Bought the Land Carter Worked as a Teenager and Returned To at 100 Jimmy Carter spent most of his life within walking distance of the same fields. He worked them beside his father, came back in 1953 after the Navy to run the family business when his father died, and kept visiting until he was physically unable to, at which point he sometimes found someone to drive him through them ( Washington Post ). He died in late 2024 at age 100. Last week, the Conservation Fund announced it had bought the farm for about $8.5 million, roughly 2,458 acres outside Plains ( The Guardian ; FOX 5 Atlanta ). Amy Carter, the former president's only daughter, said she and her three brothers decided quickly that the sale felt right. The land passes to a buyer whose stated goal is to keep it from being sold again. The Secret Service used to stay out of sight when Carter visited, Amy Carter recalled, so he could feel alone. That solitude is the part the sale gives up. The land will no longer be anyone's private retreat. The Plan Turns a Family Farm Into Hunting and Fishing Ground by 2027 The nonprofit intends to open the property for hunting, fishing and other outdoor recreation as soon as 2027, then transfer it to Georgia's natural resources department in 2028 ( The Guardian ). Georgia would fold it into the Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area, growing that area to nearly 7,000 acres. Stacy Funderburke, the Conservation Fund's vice president for the central Southeast region, said the land would be protected "in the way he would have wanted to see," and open to others who want the same connection to it ( Washington Post ). The habitat is the practical payoff. The fields and forests hold longleaf pine and threatened gopher tortoises, along with birds and other wildlife. Protecting them is the part of the deal that outlasts the ceremony. Carter's own hunting habits were modest: turkey season every spring, according to Blake Sullivan, who managed the farm and timberland for more than four decades. Sullivan said Carter "saw his job as being a good steward," and called the sale "a fitting tribute." They liked to go and walk the land. That was their escape, to get out into the woods. Blake Sullivan, longtime manager of Carter's farm It Fits a Record Carter Built in Washington The farm is not the only Carter site in Plains. The Jimmy Carter National Historical Park, run by the National Park Service, covers his boyhood home and the site of his 1976 campaign headquarters, and the sale does not touch it ( Washington Post ). The two properties now split a legacy: the federal government keeps the buildings, and the state will keep the land. The Conservation Fund drew a straight line from the farm to what Carter did as president. He signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act in late 1980, protecting more than 104 million acres, still the largest expansion of protected public land in U.S. history ( The Guardian ). He also established 39 national park system units, among them the Martin Luther King Jr. National Historic Site and the Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area in Atlanta. 104 million acres The area Carter protected in Alaska with one signature, from a man whose first lessons in land came from peanut rows. The farm that raised him will now answer to the public, with a 2027 opening date and a 2028 handoff to Georgia.

page.title: Carter's Land, Kept Public
page.contest: Whether a former president's private farm is best honored by turning it into protected public land, or whether the sale gives up the private solitude that tied the place to him.
page.stakes: The Carter family loses a private retreat, while hunters, anglers and wildlife gain a protected area of nearly 7,000 acres. Georgia takes on management of the land in 2028, and the buyer's stated aim is to keep it from being sold again.
page.here: The Conservation Fund announced it had bought the roughly 2,458-acre Carter farm for about $8.5 million, planning public hunting and fishing by 2027 and a transfer to Georgia in 2028.

stories.headline: A Republican Congressman Forced a House Vote on Impeaching Pete Hegseth. The Defense Secretary's Best Defense Is That the President Told Him To.
stories.lede: Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight impeachment articles against Pete Hegseth on Monday.
stories.truths: Massie Filed Eight Articles Against Hegseth. A Vote Could Come Within Days. Thomas Massie has nothing left to protect. A Trump-backed challenger beat him in his primary, so he leaves Congress in January, and on Monday he used the time he has left to file eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary. They cover the Iran war, the boat strikes, the Maduro capture, the Yemen campaign, and the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly over a video reminding troops they can refuse illegal orders ( Atlanta Black Star ). Hegseth disputes every charge. The arithmetic is why this one matters. Republicans hold the House 218-214, so a few defections would be enough, and Massie says several members agree with some articles but not all ( Reuters ; The Daily Beast ). Speaker Mike Johnson already sent members home early in September to avoid a vote, and Sen. Ted Cruz says the reason was simple: Republicans lacked the votes to stop it ( The Atlantic ). Now the House must act on a privileged resolution within two legislative days. Leaders are weighing a motion to table or refer it to committee, and either would let it expire Jan. 3 ( ABC News ). Conviction is a separate matter. It takes two-thirds of the Senate, and Republicans hold 53 seats ( Reuters ). Cruz is blunt about the odds on the House side: "On the face of it, the votes are there" ( The Daily Beast ). Hegseth Held His First Press Conference in Six Months. His Defense Pointed at Trump. Hegseth chose this fight to break a half-year silence with reporters, and he spent most of it talking to one viewer. He called Massie "one disgruntled and defeated congressman," called the effort a "farce" and a "stunt," and said each operation was "ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself" ( BBC ). He even borrowed Trump's own phrase for the Ukraine call that led to the 2019 impeachment: a "perfect phone call." That defense has a cost, and Marco Rubio spelled it out the next day. Asked whether the Iran, Venezuela, Yemen and drug-boat operations were lawful, Rubio said Hegseth acted on "the direct order from the Commander-in-Chief" ( Atlanta Black Star ). Neither man accused Trump of anything. But a shield made of the president's orders leads straight back to the president, which is the very place Trump spent Monday trying to steer attention away from. He told CNN's Kaitlan Collins she was "a loser" instead of answering her question about the allegations. Not everyone in Trump's orbit saw the defense as airtight. Fox News legal analyst Jonathan Turley called six of the eight articles "nonstarters," and said the two strongest, the boat strikes and the Kelly effort, are policies he criticizes but would not call impeachable ( Mediaite ). He also conceded the plain point: "So could they succeed in impeaching him? Of course they could." Republicans Lost Both Chambers. Now They're Arguing Over Whose War It Was. Behind the procedural fight sits the question Republicans would prefer to avoid. A week ago they lost the House and the Senate, and Vice President JD Vance has said flatly that voters were angry over the Iran war, the cost of living and inflation ( The Daily Beast ). Vance spent months defending the war as an administration spokesman, after building his name as the anti-interventionist wing's standard bearer. Pressed on his boss's assessment, Hegseth said politics is "not really my thing." Both men are reportedly weighing 2028, and both now need to explain a war without owning its political damage ( The Daily Beast ). Trump faces the same bind. Keeping Hegseth looks like ignoring the voters, and firing him looks like admitting the war became a liability ( BBC ). Cruz has already named his own choices: resign, be fired, or be impeached. The man who filed the articles will be gone in January. The man they target has hung his defense on a president who has not yet decided whether he is worth keeping.

stories.headline: Trump Left Biden a Warm Letter in the Oval Office. Then Came Nearly Six Years of Attacks, and a White House Statement Calling Biden "a Disgrace."
stories.lede: Biden published a warm 2021 letter from Trump; Trump's office called Biden a "disgrace."
stories.truths: Trump's Inauguration Day Letter Praised Biden's Love for the American People The letter was waiting in the Oval Office on Jan. 20, 2021. Trump had skipped Biden's swearing-in that morning and flown to Palm Beach instead, after months of personal attacks on Biden and an effort to overturn the election results ( The Daily Beast ). What he left behind read like a note from a mentor. "Coming to work every day in the Oval Office is a blessing beyond imagination," it began, and it closed with "May God bless you and Jill" ( Mediaite ). The letter carried no attacks on Biden and no challenge to the election results ( The Daily Beast ). It told Biden that many presidents "were just swept along in its relentless tide," and that this would not happen to him "because I know how much you love the American people" ( Mediaite ). Biden held it for nearly six years. Now 83 and treating an aggressive prostate cancer that spread to his bones, he reprinted it in full in his book Promise Me, America , and The New York Times obtained an excerpt ( The New York Times ). He wrote that it left him feeling "as if there were two Donald Trumps" ( The Daily Beast ). That is the part of the story that was always going to travel. The reaction to it is the part that explains what Biden was actually describing. The White House Answered With the Other Donald Trump A letter this gracious invites one obvious response from the man who wrote it. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, whose job is to answer for Trump in a single sentence, chose a different one. "Joe Biden should have heeded the president's wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies," he told the Times. "Biden is a disgrace, and America is better off with him no longer as president" ( Mediaite ). So the letter and the statement now exist side by side, both issued by Trump's office. One praises Biden's love for the American people. The other accuses him of trying to destroy them. Cheung gave the Daily Beast the same words, so the answer was prepared before the question was asked ( The Daily Beast ). Biden's account suggests the split runs in both directions. When the two men met in the Oval Office after Trump's 2024 victory, Biden writes, Trump was "immediately chatty" and so friendly that Biden "thought he might be putting me on." Trump told him that "if it weren't for politics, we'd spend all our time golfing together." Biden notes that Trump had refused him that same courtesy four years earlier ( The Daily Beast ). The warmth shows up in private, in a sealed envelope or an Oval Office chat, and the contempt shows up wherever there is a microphone. Biden, who says treatment will limit his public appearances, has handed the book the job of speaking for him. "I'm hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves," he wrote on X ( The Daily Beast ). On this one, the words on the page belong to Trump.

page.title: A Transition Letter and Its Answer
page.contest: Whether the private courtesies of a presidential transition can coexist with public denunciation of a predecessor by the same office that extended them.
page.stakes: At stake is the norm that outgoing and incoming presidents treat the handoff of power as a shared duty, a norm that officeholders and voters both rely on. For Biden and Trump, and for a public judging sincerity, the question is which version of the record counts.
page.here: Biden published Trump's warm 2021 letter in his book, and Trump's White House communications director answered by calling Biden a disgrace.
